## 10. Applications: standard theorems with nonstandard proofs

### 10.1 Robinson's criteria

Every real sequence $a : \mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{R}$ extends to hypernatural indices. Working with hyperreals ${}^\ast\mathbb{R} = \mathbb{R}^{\mathbb{N}}/\mathcal{U}$ along the same ultrafilter, define
$$ a^\ast([f]) := [\,i \mapsto a_{f(i)}\,] \in {}^\ast\mathbb{R}. $$
This agrees with $a$ on standard indices. Recall that a hyperreal $X$ has *standard part* $L\in\mathbb{R}$ (written $X \approx L$) when $|X - L| < \varepsilon$ for every real $\varepsilon>0$, and that $X$ is *positive infinite* when $X>r$ for every real $r$.

**Theorem 10.1 (Convergence).** $a_n \to L$ as $n\to\infty$ if and only if $a^\ast(H) \approx L$ for every unlimited $H$.

*Proof sketch.* ($\Rightarrow$) Given $\varepsilon>0$ choose $N$ with $|a_n-L|<\varepsilon$ for $n \ge N$. If $H=[f]$ is unlimited then $f(i)>N$ almost everywhere, so $|a_{f(i)}-L|<\varepsilon$ almost everywhere, i.e. $|a^\ast(H)-L|<\varepsilon$. ($\Leftarrow$) If $a_n \not\to L$, there is $\varepsilon>0$ and for each $i$ an index $f(i) \ge i$ with $|a_{f(i)}-L|\ge\varepsilon$. Then $[f]$ is unlimited but $|a^\ast([f])-L| \ge \varepsilon$, contradicting the hypothesis. $\square$

**Theorem 10.2 (Divergence to $+\infty$).** $a_n \to +\infty$ if and only if $a^\ast(H)$ is positive infinite for every unlimited $H$.

**Example 10.3.** The sequence $a_n=(-1)^n$ has no limit: the unlimited indices $[2i]$ and $[2i+1]$ give $a^\ast = 1$ and $a^\ast=-1$, with standard parts $1 \ne -1$.

The content of these theorems is a change of logical shape: the $\forall\varepsilon\exists N\forall n$ of the definition is replaced by a *universally quantified evaluation* over unlimited indices. Both directions are genuine transfer results; the reverse implications need choice to assemble a misbehaving unlimited index.

### 10.2 Infinitude and pigeonhole

**Theorem 10.4 (Nonstandard criterion for infinitude).** $S\subseteq\mathbb{N}$ is infinite if and only if ${}^\ast S$ contains an unlimited element.

*Proof.* If $S$ is infinite, choose $f(i)\in S$ with $f(i)>i$; then $[f]$ is unlimited and lies in ${}^\ast S$. Conversely if $S$ is finite with bound $N$ and $[f] \in {}^\ast S$ is unlimited, then almost everywhere $f(i)\in S$, so $f(i)\le N$, contradicting $f(i)>N$ almost everywhere. $\square$

**Lemma 10.5 (Ultrafilter concentration).** For any map $j:\mathbb{N}\to F$ into a finite set, there is $b \in F$ with $j(i)=b$ for almost all $i$.

*Proof.* The pushforward ultrafilter $j_\ast\mathcal{U}$ on the finite set $F$ is principal, say at $b$; then $j^{-1}(\{b\})$ is large. $\square$

**Theorem 10.6 (Infinite pigeonhole).** If $S_1,\dots,S_k \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ cover $\mathbb{N}$, some $S_j$ is infinite.

*Proof.* Choose $j(i)$ with $i \in S_{j(i)}$. By Lemma 10.5 there is $b$ with $j(i)=b$ almost everywhere, so $i \in S_b$ almost everywhere, i.e. $\omega \in {}^\ast S_b$. Since $\omega$ is unlimited, Theorem 10.4 gives that $S_b$ is infinite. $\square$

### 10.3 Bolzano–Weierstrass

**Theorem 10.7.** Every bounded real sequence has a cluster point: if $|a_n|\le C$ for all $n$, there is $L\in\mathbb{R}$ such that for all $\varepsilon>0$ and all $N$ there is $n\ge N$ with $|a_n - L|<\varepsilon$.

*Proof.* Consider $X := [\,i \mapsto a_i\,] \in {}^\ast\mathbb{R}$, the value of the sequence at the infinite index $\omega$. Since $-(C+1) < a_i < C+1$ for all $i$, $X$ is not infinite, hence has a standard part $L := \mathrm{st}(X)$. Suppose $L$ were not a cluster point: there are $\varepsilon>0$ and $N$ with $|a_n - L| \ge \varepsilon$ for all $n \ge N$. Since $\{i \ge N\}$ is large, $|a_i - L|\ge\varepsilon$ almost everywhere, so $|X - L| \ge \varepsilon$ in ${}^\ast\mathbb{R}$, contradicting $X \approx L$. $\square$

Compactness has been reduced to the *rounding* of a finite hyperreal to a real number. This is the paradigmatic nonstandard proof: an infinitary construction (a convergent subsequence) is replaced by the evaluation of a single object at a single infinite point.

---

## 11. Algorithms and computational content

Although $\mathcal{U}$ is not constructible, all the constructions above are *coordinatewise algorithmic*: each proof produces an explicit sequence, and truncating the sequence at a finite horizon gives a finite computation that exhibits the phenomenon. Three algorithms recur.

**A. Diagonal witness (overspill / saturation).** Given coordinatewise data $A_i$ (or a family $A^{(n)}_i$), compute at coordinate $i$ the *depth*
$$ d(i) = \max\{n \le i : \Pi_n(i) \neq \varnothing\},\qquad \Pi_n(i)=\bigcap_{k\le n}A^{(k)}_i, $$
and return a point of $\Pi_{d(i)}(i)$. For a single set this specializes to $\max\{k \le i : k \in A_i\}$. Cost at coordinate $i$: $O(i \cdot |A|)$ membership tests with the search bounded by $i$; the resulting sequence is unlimited whenever the data are "eventually deep". This one construction proves overspill, internal induction, internal completeness (with the bound $b(i)$ in place of $i$) and countable saturation.

**B. Slope separation (cardinality).** For $0<r<s$, the smallest coordinate at which the staircases separate is bounded by $\lceil 1/(s-r)\rceil$; from that point on $\lfloor ir\rfloor<\lfloor is\rfloor$ forever. Computing this crossing index numerically demonstrates that a continuum of pairwise distinct unlimited elements is available, and that the separation is *eventual*, never immediate.

**C. Composite-run localization (prime-free galaxies).** Given a standard bandwidth $m$, find coordinates $i$ for which the whole window $[\,i!+\lfloor i/2\rfloor-m,\ i!+\lfloor i/2\rfloor+m\,]$ is composite. By Lemma 9.9 every $i \ge 2m+8$ works, which is exactly the finite content of Theorem 9.11: the galaxy of $C$ is prime-free because every finite bandwidth is eventually swallowed by the composite run.

---

## 12. Discussion, open problems, and future directions

### 12.1 What the survey shows

Three theses are supported by the results above.

1. **Transfer is total, and therefore uninformative about pathology.** Every first-order theorem of arithmetic holds in the model (Theorem 3.1). The interesting mathematics of nonstandard models is thus entirely about the second-order layer.

2. **Internal/external is the correct dividing line.** Well-ordering, induction and completeness survive precisely in their internal forms (Theorems 5.1, 5.4, 5.7) and fail precisely in their external forms (Theorems 5.2, 5.5, 5.8). The failures are as extreme as possible: not merely "the supremum may be missing", but "no supremum exists"; not merely "the minimum may be missing", but "every element admits a strictly smaller one in the set".

3. **Some classical phenomena become geometric.** Arbitrarily long prime gaps, an asymptotic statement about $\mathbb{N}$, becomes the structural statement that whole intervals of galaxies are prime-free (Theorems 9.11, 9.12). This is the clearest instance in our survey where the nonstandard model does not merely re-encode a classical fact but reorganizes it.

### 12.2 Limitations

The results concern one specific model, an ultrapower along a nonprincipal ultrafilter on $\mathbb{N}$. Its cardinality is $\mathfrak{c}$ and its saturation is $\aleph_1$; both are optimal for this construction but not for nonstandard models in general. Whether the galaxy order is, under the continuum hypothesis, of the specific type $\mathbb{N} + \eta\cdot\mathfrak{c}$ (with $\eta$ the order type of $\mathbb{Q}$) is not settled here. Nor is the exact strength of the internal/external dividing line: we have established the dichotomy on a substantial sample of theorems rather than proving a metatheorem that explains it.

### 12.3 Future Directions

*Conjecture 1 (Saturation $\Rightarrow$ nonstandard compactness for internal families).* Every countable family of internal subsets of ${}^\ast\mathbb{N}$ with the finite intersection property has an *internal set* contained in all of them — not merely a common element as established in Theorem 8.2. Equivalently, the internal sets form a countably compact family closed under internal intersections indexed by a hypernatural. The key insight is that the diagonal depth function used in the saturation proof already produces an internal object, namely the germ of the finite intersections $\bigcap_{k \le d(i)} A^{(k)}_i$; making this precise turns countable saturation into a statement about internal families indexed by an unlimited hypernatural, i.e. into genuine "hyperfinite compactness". The diagonal witness and the internal-set machinery are already in place; only the indexing by an unlimited element is missing, and the decreasing case (Corollary 8.4) is already in reach.

*Conjecture 2 (Primes are dense on the multiplicative scale) — twice revised.* Two successive versions of this conjecture are refuted above: "every galaxy contains a hyperprime" fails (Theorem 9.11), and even "prime-carrying galaxies are dense" fails (Theorem 9.12: no galaxy strictly between the galaxies of $[i!]$ and $[i!+i]$ carries a prime). Additive scales are therefore the wrong invariant. The surviving conjecture is multiplicative: call $H$ and $K$ *commensurable* when $H \le K^n$ and $K \le H^n$ for some standard $n$; then every commensurability class of unlimited hypernaturals contains a hyperprime. The key insight is that Bertrand's postulate produces a prime in every interval $(x,2x)$ pointwise, and $[x]$ and $[2x]$ are always commensurable even though they are typically in different galaxies — so the multiplicative scale is exactly the resolution at which the prime distribution becomes uniform, while the additive (galaxy) scale is too fine. The germ-level machinery for commensurability is a direct variant of the same-galaxy relation, and the two refutations pin down precisely why the additive version fails.

*Conjecture 3 (Galaxy order type is that of a nonstandard model of arithmetic).* The quotient of ${}^\ast\mathbb{N}$ by the same-galaxy relation is a dense linear order without endpoints above its least element, and it is order-isomorphic to a quotient of size exactly $\mathfrak{c}$. Density (Theorem 7.5), unboundedness (Theorems 7.6, 7.7) and the least element (Theorem 7.4) are established; what remains is the cardinality of the quotient and, under the continuum hypothesis, the isomorphism type $\mathbb{N} + \eta\cdot\mathfrak{c}$.

Further natural targets suggested by the present work: an internal version of the prime number theorem (what is the internal density of hyperprimes below an unlimited $H$?); a systematic metatheorem characterizing which second-order principles survive internally; the behavior of the model under iterated ultrapowers, where saturation can be increased beyond $\aleph_1$; and a nonstandard treatment of Ramsey-type theorems along the lines of the pigeonhole proof of Theorem 10.6, where the ultrafilter concentration lemma replaces a compactness argument.

---

## 13. Conclusion

We have exhibited a concrete non-Archimedean model of arithmetic and mapped, theorem by theorem, what classical mathematics survives inside it. First-order arithmetic transfers completely; the classical set-theoretic principles of $\mathbb{N}$ survive exactly in their internal forms and fail maximally in their external forms; the model has the cardinality of the continuum and a densely stratified order of scales; countable saturation supplies a compactness that $\mathbb{N}$ itself lacks; elementary number theory transfers in force, including Euclidean division with uniqueness, gcd's, sharp Euclid, Fermat and Wilson; but the primes are not spread uniformly across scales, and whole intervals of galaxies are prime-free. In the other direction, the model repays the effort: convergence becomes evaluation at an infinite index, infinitude becomes membership, pigeonhole becomes ultrafilter concentration, and Bolzano–Weierstrass becomes rounding. The alien arithmetic is indistinguishable from ours in what it can *say*, radically different in what it *contains*, and useful precisely because of the gap.

interval of galaxies containing no hyperprime, so the prime-carrying galaxies are not dense.
As applications we give nonstandard proofs of the infinite pigeonhole principle and of the
Bolzano--Weierstrass theorem, and prove Robinson's characterizations of convergence and
divergence for real sequences.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}

Ordinary arithmetic is not categorical: there are models of the first-order theory of
$\mathbb{N}$ containing elements larger than every numeral. Such models are usually invoked
abstractly. This paper instead studies one \emph{concrete} model in detail, an ultrapower of
$\mathbb{N}$, and asks a systematic question: taking the classical theorems of elementary
arithmetic and analysis one at a time, which survive, in what form, and why do the others fail?

The answer has an unexpectedly clean shape. Everything expressible in the first-order language
of arithmetic survives, by transfer, and this is not the interesting part. The interesting part
is the second-order corpus, where the model bifurcates. Every subset of $\hN$ is either
\emph{internal} (assembled coordinatewise from ordinary sets) or \emph{external}. Our central
finding, established across a dozen theorems, is that classical set-theoretic principles of
arithmetic survive for internal sets and fail for external ones, and the failures are as violent
as each statement permits. In the number-theoretic direction we find one genuine surprise:
unboundedness of primes transfers, but equidistribution across scales does not.

\section{The model}

\begin{definition}[Ultrafilter]
A \emph{filter} on $\mathbb{N}$ is a nonempty family $\mathcal{F}$ of subsets of $\mathbb{N}$
closed under supersets and finite intersections with $\varnothing\notin\mathcal{F}$. An
\emph{ultrafilter} is a filter $\mathcal{U}$ such that for every $S\subseteq\mathbb{N}$, either
$S\in\mathcal{U}$ or $\mathbb{N}\setminus S\in\mathcal{U}$. It is \emph{nonprincipal} when it
contains no finite set; equivalently it contains every cofinite set.
\end{definition}

Throughout, $\mathcal{U}$ is a fixed nonprincipal ultrafilter on $\mathbb{N}$, whose existence
follows from Zorn's lemma. We call $S$ \emph{large} when $S\in\mathcal{U}$ and write
$\allae i,\ P(i)$ for ``$\{i:P(i)\}$ is large'' (``$P$ holds for almost all $i$''). We use
constantly: (i) finite intersections of large sets are large; (ii)
$\neg\allae i\,P(i)\iff\allae i\,\neg P(i)$; (iii) $\allae i,\ i\ge m$ for every $m$.

\begin{definition}
For $f,g:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}$ set $f\sim g$ iff $\allae i,\ f(i)=g(i)$; the quotient
$\hN=\mathbb{N}^{\mathbb{N}}/\!\sim$ is the set of \emph{hypernaturals}, with $[f]$ the germ of
$f$. Operations and relations are lifted pointwise:
$[f]+[g]=[i\mapsto f(i)+g(i)]$, $[f]\cdot[g]=[i\mapsto f(i)g(i)]$ and
$[f]<[g]\iff\allae i,\ f(i)<g(i)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}
$(\hN,+,\cdot,<)$ is a linearly ordered commutative semiring and $n\mapsto n^{\ast}:=[i\mapsto n]$
is an injective embedding preserving operations and order.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Algebraic identities hold pointwise. Linearity of the order uses the ultrafilter dichotomy:
the three sets on which $f<g$, $f=g$, $f>g$ partition $\mathbb{N}$, and a filter cannot contain
two disjoint sets, so exactly one is large. Injectivity holds because no finite set is large.
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}
$H\in\hN$ is \emph{standard} if $H=n^{\ast}$ for some $n$, and \emph{unlimited} if $n^{\ast}<H$
for all $n\in\mathbb{N}$. Write $\omega:=[i\mapsto i]$.
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}
$\omega$ is unlimited; unlimited elements are not standard; and $[f]$ is unlimited iff for every
$n$ one has $f(i)>n$ for almost all $i$.
\end{proposition}

Thus $\hN$ is non-Archimedean.

\section{Transfer}

\begin{theorem}[Transfer principle, \L o\'s]\label{thm:los}
Let $L$ be a first-order language, $M$ a nonempty $L$-structure, $\mathcal{U}$ an ultrafilter on
an index set $I$, and ${}^{\ast}M=M^{I}/\mathcal{U}$. Then for every $L$-sentence $\varphi$,
${}^{\ast}M\models\varphi$ iff $M\models\varphi$; hence ${}^{\ast}M\equiv M$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
One proves, by induction on formulas $\varphi(x_1,\dots,x_k)$, that
${}^{\ast}M\models\varphi([f_1],\dots,[f_k])$ iff
$\allae i,\ M\models\varphi(f_1(i),\dots,f_k(i))$. Atomic cases hold by definition; conjunction
uses finite intersections; negation uses the ultrafilter dichotomy (the only place where
``ultra'' is needed); the existential step uses the axiom of choice to assemble a witnessing
germ from coordinatewise witnesses. For a sentence the right-hand side is a constant condition.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}
$\hN$ satisfies every first-order theorem of arithmetic: the order is discrete with least
element, successors exist, every element $>1$ has a prime divisor, primes are unbounded,
Euclidean division exists, and so on.
\end{corollary}

\begin{definition}[Internal set]
An \emph{internal subset} of $\hN$ is a germ $[A]$ of a sequence $A:\mathbb{N}\to
\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{N})$, with
\[
[f]\in^{\ast}[A]\quad:\iff\quad\allae i,\ f(i)\in A_i .
\]
A subset not of this form is \emph{external}. For $S\subseteq\mathbb{N}$ the
\emph{star-extension} ${}^{\ast}S$ is given by the constant sequence $A_i=S$.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:compl}
$[f]\in^{\ast}[A^{c}]$ iff $[f]\notin^{\ast}[A]$, where $A^{c}_i=\mathbb{N}\setminus A_i$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{theorem}[Universal transfer]\label{thm:univ}
$\bigl(\forall H\in\hN,\ H\in^{\ast}[A]\bigr)\iff\allae i,\ A_i=\mathbb{N}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
($\Leftarrow$) is immediate. For ($\Rightarrow$), if the right side fails then, by dichotomy,
for almost all $i$ there is $x\notin A_i$; choose $g(i)$ to be such an $x$. Then
$[g]\notin^{\ast}[A]$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Existential transfer]\label{thm:exists}
$\bigl(\exists H,\ H\in^{\ast}[A]\bigr)\iff\allae i,\ A_i\neq\varnothing$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proposition}[Internal induction from transfer]
If for almost all $i$ the set $A_i$ contains $0$ and is closed under successor, then
$H\in^{\ast}[A]$ for every $H$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Ordinary induction gives $A_i=\mathbb{N}$ for such $i$; apply Theorem~\ref{thm:univ}.
\end{proof}

\section{Spilling and the externality of the standard cut}

\begin{theorem}[Overspill]\label{thm:overspill}
If an internal set $[A]$ contains $n^{\ast}$ for every $n\in\mathbb{N}$, it contains an unlimited
element.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Set $f(i):=\max\{k\le i: k\in A_i\}$ (and $0$ if none). Fix $n$: for almost all $i$ we have
$n+1\in A_i$ and $i\ge n+1$, so $f(i)\ge n+1$; hence $[f]$ is unlimited. Also for almost all $i$
we have $1\in A_i$ and $i\ge1$, so $f(i)\in A_i$; hence $[f]\in^{\ast}[A]$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Underspill]
If an internal set contains every unlimited hypernatural, it contains a standard one.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Otherwise $n^{\ast}\in^{\ast}[A^{c}]$ for all $n$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:compl}; overspill gives an
unlimited element of $[A^{c}]$, contradicting the hypothesis.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[The standard cut is external]
No internal set has exactly the standard hypernaturals as members; likewise none has exactly
the unlimited ones.
\end{theorem}

\section{The survival/failure dichotomy}

\begin{theorem}[Internal well-ordering]\label{thm:lnp}
Every nonempty internal set has a least element.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
If $[g]\in^{\ast}[A]$ then $A_i\ne\varnothing$ almost everywhere; put $s(i):=\min A_i$. Then
$[s]\in^{\ast}[A]$, and $[k]\in^{\ast}[A]$ implies $s(i)\le k(i)$ almost everywhere.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[External failure]\label{thm:noleast}
For every unlimited $H$ there is an unlimited $K<H$. Hence the unlimited elements have no least
element, and form an external set.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
With $H=[f]$, take $K=[i\mapsto f(i)-1]$ (truncated subtraction): for each $n$, almost everywhere
$f(i)>n+1$, so $f(i)-1>n$, and almost everywhere $f(i)>0$, so $f(i)-1<f(i)$. If the unlimited
part were internal it would have a least element by Theorem~\ref{thm:lnp}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Internal induction]
If $[A]$ is internal, $0^{\ast}\in^{\ast}[A]$, and $H\in^{\ast}[A]\Rightarrow H+1\in^{\ast}[A]$
for all $H$, then $H\in^{\ast}[A]$ for all $H$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Suppose $[h]\notin^{\ast}[A]$; by dichotomy $h(i)\notin A_i$ almost everywhere while $0\in A_i$
almost everywhere. Put $c(i):=\max\{k\le h(i):k\in A_i\}$. Then $c(i)\in A_i$, $c(i)\neq h(i)$,
so $c(i)+1\le h(i)$ and by maximality $c(i)+1\notin A_i$. Thus $[c]\in^{\ast}[A]$ while
$[c]+1\notin^{\ast}[A]$, contradicting closure under successor.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[External failure of induction]
$0^{\ast}$ is standard, the successor of a standard element is standard, yet $\omega$ is not
standard.
\end{theorem}

\begin{lemma}[Bound transfer]\label{lem:bound}
If every $H\in^{\ast}[A]$ satisfies $H\le[b]$, then for almost all $i$ every $x\in A_i$ satisfies
$x\le b(i)$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Otherwise, by dichotomy, $B_i:=\{x\in A_i:x>b(i)\}$ is nonempty for almost all $i$; by
Theorem~\ref{thm:exists} there is $[g]\in^{\ast}[B]$, which lies in $[A]$ and hence satisfies
$g(i)\le b(i)$ almost everywhere, contradicting $g(i)>b(i)$ almost everywhere.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Internal completeness]
A nonempty internal set bounded above has a greatest element, which is its least upper bound.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
With $[b]$ an upper bound, Lemma~\ref{lem:bound} lets us set $s(i):=\max\{x\le b(i):x\in A_i\}$,
well defined almost everywhere. Then $[s]\in^{\ast}[A]$ dominates every member and, being a
member, lies below every upper bound.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[External failure of completeness]
The standard cut is bounded above by $\omega$ but has no least upper bound.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Any upper bound $S$ satisfies $n^{\ast}<(n+1)^{\ast}\le S$ for all $n$, hence is unlimited; by
Theorem~\ref{thm:noleast} there is an unlimited $K<S$, still an upper bound.
\end{proof}

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{lll}
\toprule
Classical principle & Internal form & External form\\
\midrule
Least number principle & holds & fails maximally\\
Induction & holds & fails for ``is standard''\\
Bounded sets have suprema & holds, with maxima & no supremum exists\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\section{The size of the model}

\begin{theorem}\label{thm:card}
$|\hN|=\mathfrak{c}$. Moreover the set of unlimited elements has cardinality $\mathfrak{c}$ and
the standard part has cardinality $\aleph_0$; in particular $\hN$ is uncountable and admits no
bijection with $\mathbb{N}$.
\end{theorem}

The upper bound is immediate since $\hN$ is a quotient of $\mathbb{N}^{\mathbb{N}}$ and
$\aleph_0^{\aleph_0}=\mathfrak{c}$. For the lower bound:

\begin{definition}
For real $r>0$ let $S_r:=[\,i\mapsto\lfloor ir\rfloor\,]\in\hN$.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}
$S_r$ is unlimited for every $r>0$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Fix $c$ and pick $N>(c+1)/r$, so $c+1<Nr$. For $i\ge N$, $c+1\le ir$, hence
$c+1\le\lfloor ir\rfloor$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Slope separation]
If $0<r<s$ then $S_r<S_s$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Pick $N>1/(s-r)$. For $i\ge N$ we get $1<i(s-r)$, i.e. $ir+1<is$; since
$\lfloor ir\rfloor\le ir$ we get $\lfloor ir\rfloor+1\le is$ and hence
$\lfloor ir\rfloor<\lfloor is\rfloor$. The set $\{i\ge N\}$ is large.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}
$r\mapsto S_r$ is a strictly increasing injection of $(0,\infty)$ into the unlimited elements,
which proves Theorem~\ref{thm:card}.
\end{corollary}

\begin{remark}
Together with Theorem~\ref{thm:los} this is the sharpest illustration of the weakness of
first-order expressibility: $\hN\equiv\mathbb{N}$, yet the two are not even equinumerous.
\end{remark}

\section{Galaxies: the order type of the model}

\begin{definition}
$H\approx K$ (\emph{same galaxy}) iff $K\le H+n^{\ast}$ and $H\le K+n^{\ast}$ for some
$n\in\mathbb{N}$; and $H\prec K$ (\emph{$K$ far above $H$}) iff $H+n^{\ast}<K$ for all
$n\in\mathbb{N}$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}
$\approx$ is an equivalence relation and a congruence for addition. Moreover $H\prec K$ implies
$H<K$; $\prec$ is irreflexive and transitive; for $H<K$ one has $H\prec K$ iff $H\not\approx K$;
and $\prec$ is invariant under $\approx$ in both arguments. Hence $\prec$ induces a strict linear
order on galaxies.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Least galaxy]
$0^{\ast}\prec H$ iff $H$ is unlimited, and every unlimited $H$ satisfies $m^{\ast}\prec H$ for
all standard $m$. Thus the standard galaxy is least.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Density]
If $H\prec K$ then there is $M$ with $H\prec M\prec K$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Take $M:=[\,i\mapsto f(i)+\lfloor(g(i)-f(i))/2\rfloor\,]$; given $n$, apply the hypothesis with
$2n+2$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[No greatest and no least nonstandard galaxy]
$H\prec H+\omega$ for every $H$; and if $H$ is unlimited then
$K:=[\,i\mapsto\lfloor f(i)/2\rfloor\,]$ is unlimited with $K\prec H$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{corollary}
There is an infinite strictly descending chain of galaxies of unlimited elements, e.g.
$\omega\succ\lfloor\omega/2\rfloor\succ\lfloor\omega/4\rfloor\succ\cdots$. The galaxy order is
$\mathbb{N}$ followed by a dense order without endpoints.
\end{corollary}

\section{Countable saturation}

\begin{theorem}[$\aleph_1$-saturation]\label{thm:sat}
Let $\{[A^{(n)}]\}_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ be internal subsets of $\hN$ such that every finite
subfamily has a common element. Then there is $H$ with $H\in^{\ast}[A^{(n)}]$ for all $n$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Let $\Pi_n(i):=\bigcap_{k\le n}A^{(k)}_i$.
\emph{Step 1:} for each $n$, $\Pi_n(i)\neq\varnothing$ for almost all $i$, since a witness germ
for the first $n+1$ conditions gives $n+1$ large sets whose (finite) intersection is large.
\emph{Step 2:} define the depth $d(i):=\max\{n\le i:\Pi_n(i)\neq\varnothing\}$ and let $f(i)$ be
a point of $\Pi_{d(i)}(i)$ (or $0$).
\emph{Step 3:} fix $n$; for almost all $i$ we have $\Pi_0(i)\neq\varnothing$,
$\Pi_n(i)\neq\varnothing$ and $i\ge n$, whence $d(i)\ge n$ and
$f(i)\in\Pi_{d(i)}(i)\subseteq A^{(n)}_i$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}
Overspill follows by applying Theorem~\ref{thm:sat} to the conditions
$B^{(n)}_i=\{x\in A_i:x>n\}$. Moreover a decreasing chain of nonempty internal sets has a common
element --- in sharp contrast with $\mathbb{N}$, where $\bigcap_n\{k:k\ge n\}=\varnothing$.
\end{corollary}

\section{Number theory in the model}

Truncated subtraction, exponentiation with hypernatural exponent, and factorial are lifted
coordinatewise: $A\ominus B=[a(i)-b(i)]$, $A^{B}=[a(i)^{b(i)}]$, $A!=[a(i)!]$. Divisibility is
the lifted relation, and $P$ is a \emph{hyperprime} iff $p(i)$ is prime for almost all $i$.

\begin{theorem}
The germ $[\,i\mapsto p_i\,]$ of the sequence of primes is an unlimited hyperprime.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Sharp Euclid]
For every $H$ there is a hyperprime $P>H$ that is least among hyperprimes exceeding $H$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The internal set $A_i:=\{p\ \text{prime}: p>f(i)\}$ is nonempty in every coordinate, and its
members are exactly the hyperprimes exceeding $H$; apply Theorem~\ref{thm:lnp}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Fermat, doubly nonstandard]
$P\mid A^{P}\ominus A$ for every hypernatural $A$ and hyperprime $P$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Wilson]
$P\mid (P\ominus 1)!+1$ for every hyperprime $P$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Parity]
No unlimited hyperprime is divisible by $2^{\ast}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Euclidean division with uniqueness]
For $B\ne0$ and any $A$ there are unique $Q,R$ with $A=BQ+R$ and $R<B$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Take $Q=[a(i)\ \mathrm{div}\ b(i)]$, $R=[a(i)\bmod b(i)]$; both the identity and the inequality
hold coordinatewise, and pointwise uniqueness of division transfers.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}
$\gcd(A,B):=[\gcd(a(i),b(i))]$ divides $A$ and $B$ and is divisible by every common divisor.
Every $A>1^{\ast}$ has a hyperprime divisor, namely $[\mathrm{minFac}(a(i))]$.
\end{theorem}

\subsection*{Primes are not distributed across all scales}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:runs}
For $2\le j\le i$ the number $i!+j$ is composite, since $j\mid i!+j$ and $1<j<i!+j$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{theorem}[Prime-free galaxy]\label{thm:pfg}
Let $C:=[\,i\mapsto i!+\lfloor i/2\rfloor\,]$. Then $C$ is unlimited and no hyperprime lies in
the galaxy of $C$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Unlimitedness follows from $i!\ge i$. Suppose $P=[p]$ is a hyperprime with $P\approx C$,
witnessed by $m$. Restricting to the large set $\{i\ge 2m+8\}$ and writing $j(i)=p(i)-i!$, the
two galaxy inequalities force $2\le j(i)\le i$ almost everywhere, so $p(i)=i!+j(i)$ is composite
by Lemma~\ref{lem:runs}, contradicting primality on a large set.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[An interval of prime-free galaxies]
Let $H=[\,i\mapsto i!\,]$ and $K=[\,i\mapsto i!+i\,]$. Then $H\prec K$ and no hyperprime $P$
satisfies $H\prec P\prec K$. Hence the prime-carrying galaxies are not dense in the galaxy order.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Apply the two far-relations with $n=3$ and restrict to $\{i\ge8\}$: almost everywhere
$2\le p(i)-i!\le i$, and Lemma~\ref{lem:runs} applies.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}
Some galaxies do carry hyperprimes: the galaxy of $[\,i\mapsto p_i\,]$ contains one.
\end{theorem}

\section{Applications: standard theorems with nonstandard proofs}

Working with hyperreals $\hR=\mathbb{R}^{\mathbb{N}}/\mathcal{U}$ along the same ultrafilter,
every real sequence $a$ extends to $a^{\ast}([f]):=[\,i\mapsto a_{f(i)}\,]$, agreeing with $a$ at
standard indices. A hyperreal $X$ has standard part $L$ ($X\approx L$) when $|X-L|<\varepsilon$
for every real $\varepsilon>0$.

\begin{theorem}[Robinson's criterion for convergence]
$a_n\to L$ iff $a^{\ast}(H)\approx L$ for every unlimited $H$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
($\Rightarrow$) If $|a_n-L|<\varepsilon$ for $n\ge N$ and $H=[f]$ is unlimited, then $f(i)>N$
almost everywhere. ($\Leftarrow$) If $a_n\not\to L$, pick $\varepsilon>0$ and $f(i)\ge i$ with
$|a_{f(i)}-L|\ge\varepsilon$; then $[f]$ is unlimited and violates the hypothesis.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Divergence]
$a_n\to+\infty$ iff $a^{\ast}(H)$ exceeds every real for every unlimited $H$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{example}
$(-1)^n$ has no limit: the unlimited indices $[2i]$ and $[2i+1]$ give values $1$ and $-1$.
\end{example}

\begin{theorem}[Nonstandard criterion for infinitude]
$S\subseteq\mathbb{N}$ is infinite iff ${}^{\ast}S$ contains an unlimited element.
\end{theorem}

\begin{lemma}[Ultrafilter concentration]
For any $j:\mathbb{N}\to F$ with $F$ finite there is $b\in F$ with $j(i)=b$ for almost all $i$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{theorem}[Infinite pigeonhole]
If finitely many sets $S_1,\dots,S_k$ cover $\mathbb{N}$, one of them is infinite.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Choose $j(i)$ with $i\in S_{j(i)}$ and let $b$ be the concentration value; then
$\omega\in{}^{\ast}S_b$ and $\omega$ is unlimited.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Bolzano--Weierstrass]
If $|a_n|\le C$ for all $n$, there is $L\in\mathbb{R}$ such that for all $\varepsilon>0$ and all
$N$ there is $n\ge N$ with $|a_n-L|<\varepsilon$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
$X:=[\,i\mapsto a_i\,]$ satisfies $-(C+1)<X<C+1$, hence is finite and has a standard part
$L=\st(X)$. If $L$ were not a cluster point, some $\varepsilon>0$ and $N$ would give
$|a_n-L|\ge\varepsilon$ for all $n\ge N$; since $\{i\ge N\}$ is large this yields
$|X-L|\ge\varepsilon$, contradicting $X\approx L$.
\end{proof}

\section{Algorithms and computational content}

Although $\mathcal{U}$ is not constructible, every proof above produces an explicit sequence, and
truncating at a finite horizon gives a finite computation exhibiting the phenomenon.

\paragraph{A. Diagonal witness.} Compute at coordinate $i$ the depth
$d(i)=\max\{n\le i:\Pi_n(i)\neq\varnothing\}$ with $\Pi_n(i)=\bigcap_{k\le n}A^{(k)}_i$, and
return a point of $\Pi_{d(i)}(i)$; for a single set this is $\max\{k\le i:k\in A_i\}$. This one
construction proves overspill, internal induction, internal completeness (with $b(i)$ in place of
$i$) and countable saturation.

\paragraph{B. Slope separation.} For $0<r<s$ the crossing index is at most
$\lceil 1/(s-r)\rceil$; beyond it $\lfloor ir\rfloor<\lfloor is\rfloor$ forever. This exhibits a
continuum of distinct unlimited elements and shows the separation is eventual, never immediate.

\paragraph{C. Composite-run localization.} For a bandwidth $m$, every $i\ge 2m+8$ makes the whole
window $[\,i!+\lfloor i/2\rfloor-m,\ i!+\lfloor i/2\rfloor+m\,]$ composite: the finite content of
Theorem~\ref{thm:pfg}.

\section{Discussion and future directions}

Three theses are supported. First, transfer is total and therefore uninformative about pathology.
Second, internal/external is the correct dividing line: well-ordering, induction and completeness
survive precisely in internal form and fail maximally in external form. Third, some classical
phenomena become geometric --- arbitrarily long prime gaps become the statement that whole
intervals of galaxies are prime-free.

\begin{conjecture}[Hyperfinite compactness]
Every countable family of internal subsets of $\hN$ with the finite intersection property has an
\emph{internal set} contained in all of them, not merely a common element. The diagonal depth
function already produces an internal object, namely the germ of the finite intersections
$\bigcap_{k\le d(i)}A^{(k)}_i$; making this precise turns countable saturation into a statement
about internal families indexed by an unlimited hypernatural.
\end{conjecture}

\begin{conjecture}[Primes are dense on the multiplicative scale]
Call $H$ and $K$ \emph{commensurable} when $H\le K^{n}$ and $K\le H^{n}$ for some standard $n$.
Then every commensurability class of unlimited hypernaturals contains a hyperprime. Bertrand's
postulate produces a prime in every interval $(x,2x)$ pointwise, and $[x]$ and $[2x]$ are always
commensurable though typically in different galaxies: the multiplicative scale is the resolution
at which prime distribution becomes uniform, while the additive scale is too fine.
\end{conjecture}

\begin{conjecture}[Galaxy order type]
The quotient of $\hN$ by the same-galaxy relation is a dense linear order without endpoints above
its least element, of size exactly $\mathfrak{c}$, and, under the continuum hypothesis, of
isomorphism type $\mathbb{N}+\eta\cdot\mathfrak{c}$.
\end{conjecture}

Further natural targets: an internal prime number theorem (the internal density of hyperprimes
below an unlimited $H$); a metatheorem characterizing which second-order principles survive
internally; iterated ultrapowers with saturation beyond $\aleph_1$; and nonstandard treatments of
Ramsey-type theorems in which ultrafilter concentration replaces compactness.

\section{Conclusion}

We exhibited a concrete non-Archimedean model of arithmetic and mapped, theorem by theorem, what
classical mathematics survives inside it. First-order arithmetic transfers completely; the
classical set principles survive exactly in internal form and fail maximally externally; the model
has cardinality $\mathfrak{c}$ and a densely stratified order of scales; countable saturation
supplies a compactness $\mathbb{N}$ lacks; elementary number theory transfers in force; yet primes
are not spread uniformly across scales. In the other direction, the model repays the effort:
convergence becomes evaluation at an infinite index, infinitude becomes membership, pigeonhole
becomes ultrafilter concentration, and Bolzano--Weierstrass becomes rounding.

A hypernatural is an equivalence class of sequences of naturals, two sequences
being identified when they agree on a "large" set of coordinates (a set in a
fixed nonprincipal ultrafilter).  The ultrafilter itself is not constructible,

from typing import Callable, Dict, List, Optional, Sequence, Set, Tuple

# 1. Germs, order, standard elements and omega
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def eventually_threshold(pred: Callable[[int], bool],
                         horizon: int = HORIZON,
                         run: int = 40) -> Optional[int]:
    """Smallest N <= horizon such that pred(i) holds for every i in [N, horizon],
    provided the certified run has length at least `run`.  Returns None if no
    such N exists inside the horizon.  A cofinite set is large in every
    nonprincipal ultrafilter, so a genuine threshold certifies "almost all i"."""
    last_failure = -1
    for i in range(horizon + 1):
        if not pred(i):
            last_failure = i
    n = last_failure + 1
    if n > horizon - run:
        return None
    return n


def standard(n: int) -> Seq:
    """The standard hypernatural n* = [i |-> n]."""
    return lambda i: n


def omega(i: int) -> int:
    """The unlimited hypernatural omega = [i |-> i]."""
    return i


def is_unlimited(f: Seq, levels: int = 12, horizon: int = HORIZON) -> bool:
    """[f] is unlimited iff for every standard n, f(i) > n for almost all i.
    We certify the first `levels` values of n by explicit thresholds."""
    return all(eventually_threshold(lambda i, n=n: f(i) > n, horizon) is not None
               for n in range(levels))


def germ_lt(f: Seq, g: Seq, horizon: int = HORIZON) -> bool:
    """[f] < [g], certified by a threshold beyond which f(i) < g(i) always."""
    return eventually_threshold(lambda i: f(i) < g(i), horizon) is not None

def staircase(r: float) -> Seq:
    """S_r = [i |-> floor(i * r)], unlimited for every r > 0."""

def predicted_crossing(r: float, s: float) -> int:
    """Theoretical bound on the coordinate beyond which floor(i r) < floor(i s):
    any i > 1 / (s - r) works."""
    return math.ceil(1.0 / (s - r))

def far_above(f: Seq, g: Seq, levels: int = 8, horizon: int = HORIZON) -> bool:
    """[f] < [g] in the strong sense: f(i) + n < g(i) almost everywhere, for
    every standard n.  Equivalently, g lies in a strictly higher galaxy."""
    return all(eventually_threshold(lambda i, n=n: f(i) + n < g(i), horizon) is not None
               for n in range(levels))


def same_galaxy(f: Seq, g: Seq, max_shift: int = 64, horizon: int = HORIZON) -> bool:
    """[f] ~ [g] iff |f - g| stays bounded by a *standard* constant a.e."""
    for n in range(max_shift + 1):
        ok_1 = eventually_threshold(lambda i, n=n: g(i) <= f(i) + n, horizon)
        ok_2 = eventually_threshold(lambda i, n=n: f(i) <= g(i) + n, horizon)
        if ok_1 is not None and ok_2 is not None:
            return True
    return False


def midpoint(f: Seq, g: Seq) -> Seq:
    """The witness of density of the galaxy order: f + (g - f)/2."""
    return lambda i: f(i) + (g(i) - f(i)) // 2


def halve(f: Seq) -> Seq:
    """Halving drops an unlimited element into a strictly lower galaxy."""
    return lambda i: f(i) // 2

# 4. The diagonal witness: overspill and countable saturation

def diagonal_witness(membership: Callable[[int, int], bool], i: int) -> int:
    """max{ k <= i : k in A_i }  (0 if none).  This single construction proves
    overspill, internal induction and internal completeness."""
    for k in range(i, -1, -1):
        if membership(k, i):
            return k
    return 0


def saturation_witness(conditions: Sequence[Callable[[int, int], bool]],
                       i: int, search: int = 200) -> Tuple[int, int]:
    """Diagonal for countable saturation: at coordinate i satisfy as many of the
    first conditions as that coordinate allows.  Returns (depth, witness)."""
    best_depth, best_x = -1, 0
    for n in range(min(i, len(conditions) - 1), -1, -1):
        for x in range(search):
            if all(conditions[k](x, i) for k in range(n + 1)):
                return n, x
        if best_depth < 0:
            best_depth, best_x = n, 0
    return max(best_depth, 0), best_x

def is_prime(n: int) -> bool:
    if n < 2:
        return False
    if n % 2 == 0:
        return n == 2
    d = 3
    while d * d <= n:
        if n % d == 0:
            return False
        d += 2
    return True


_PRIME_CACHE: List[int] = [2]


def nth_prime(k: int) -> int:
    """The k-th prime (0-indexed), with memoization."""
    n = _PRIME_CACHE[-1]
    while len(_PRIME_CACHE) <= k:
        n += 1
        if is_prime(n):
            _PRIME_CACHE.append(n)
    return _PRIME_CACHE[k]


def min_fac(n: int) -> int:
    if n < 2:
        return n
    d = 2
    while d * d <= n:
        if n % d == 0:
            return d
        d += 1
    return n

def composite_centre(i: int) -> int:
    """C = [i |-> i! + i//2], the middle of the composite run i!+2, ..., i!+i."""
    return math.factorial(i) + i // 2


def galaxy_window_is_prime_free(i: int, bandwidth: int) -> bool:
    """Is the whole window C(i) +- bandwidth composite?"""
    c = composite_centre(i)
    return all(not is_prime(c + delta) for delta in range(-bandwidth, bandwidth + 1))


def section_6() -> None:
    print("=" * 78)
    print("6.  Prime-free galaxies: whole scales that primes never visit")
    print("=" * 78)

    print("  galaxy of [i |-> p_i]; but between the galaxies of [i!] and [i!+i]")
    print("  there is no prime-carrying galaxy at all.")
    print()

# 7. Robinson's criterion and Bolzano-Weierstrass
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def star_seq(a: Callable[[int], float], f: Seq) -> Callable[[int], float]:
    """The nonstandard extension of the real sequence a, evaluated at [f]."""
    return lambda i: a(f(i))


def standard_part_estimate(x: Callable[[int], float],
                           horizon: int = HORIZON) -> Tuple[float, float]:
    """Estimate the standard part of a hyperreal germ by the tail of its
    coordinates, together with the tail oscillation (0 means a genuine limit)."""
    tail = [x(i) for i in range(horizon // 2, horizon)]
    return sum(tail) / len(tail), max(tail) - min(tail)


def section_7() -> None:
    print("=" * 78)
    print("7.  Robinson's criterion and nonstandard Bolzano-Weierstrass")
    print("=" * 78)
    a: Callable[[int], float] = lambda n: 1.0 + 1.0 / (n + 1)
    for name, idx in [("omega", omega), ("2*omega", lambda i: 2 * i),
                      ("omega^2", lambda i: i * i)]:
        st, osc = standard_part_estimate(star_seq(a, idx))
        print(f"  a_n = 1 + 1/(n+1)   at index {name:<8}: st = {st:.6f}, "
              f"tail spread = {osc:.2e}")
    print("  -> the same standard part 1 at every unlimited index: a_n -> 1.")
    print()
    b: Callable[[int], float] = lambda n: (-1.0) ** n
    st_even, _ = standard_part_estimate(star_seq(b, lambda i: 2 * i))
    st_odd, _ = standard_part_estimate(star_seq(b, lambda i: 2 * i + 1))
    print(f"  b_n = (-1)^n  at index [2i]   : st = {st_even:+.1f}")
    print(f"  b_n = (-1)^n  at index [2i+1] : st = {st_odd:+.1f}")
    print("  -> two unlimited indices give different standard parts, so (-1)^n")
    print("     diverges.  No subsequence bookkeeping required.")
    print()
    c: Callable[[int], float] = lambda n: math.sin(n)
    x = star_seq(c, omega)          # the value at the infinite index omega
    bound = max(abs(c(i)) for i in range(HORIZON))
    print(f"  c_n = sin(n) is bounded by {bound:.4f}, so its value at the infinite")
    print("  index omega is a *finite* hyperreal and can be rounded to a real L;")
    print("  that L is automatically a cluster point (Bolzano-Weierstrass).")
    L = x(HORIZON - 1)
    hits = [n for n in range(HORIZON, 3 * HORIZON) if abs(c(n) - L) < 0.01]
    print(f"    rounding at a large coordinate gives L = {L:+.6f}")
    print(f"    indices n >= {HORIZON} with |c_n - L| < 0.01: {hits[:8]} ...")
    print("    -> the value returns to within epsilon of L infinitely often.")
    print()

def far_above(f: Seq, g: Seq, levels: int = 8, horizon: int = HORIZON) -> bool:
    """[f] < [g] in the strong sense: f(i) + n < g(i) almost everywhere, for
    every standard n.  Equivalently, g lies in a strictly higher galaxy."""
    return all(eventually_threshold(lambda i, n=n: f(i) + n < g(i), horizon) is not None
               for n in range(levels))


def same_galaxy(f: Seq, g: Seq, max_shift: int = 64, horizon: int = HORIZON) -> bool:
    """[f] ~ [g] iff |f - g| stays bounded by a *standard* constant a.e."""
    for n in range(max_shift + 1):
        ok_1 = eventually_threshold(lambda i, n=n: g(i) <= f(i) + n, horizon)
        ok_2 = eventually_threshold(lambda i, n=n: f(i) <= g(i) + n, horizon)
        if ok_1 is not None and ok_2 is not None:
            return True
    return False


def midpoint(f: Seq, g: Seq) -> Seq:
    """The witness of density of the galaxy order: f + (g - f)/2."""
    return lambda i: f(i) + (g(i) - f(i)) // 2


def halve(f: Seq) -> Seq:
    """Halving drops an unlimited element into a strictly lower galaxy."""
    return lambda i: f(i) // 2

def diagonal_witness(membership: Callable[[int, int], bool], i: int) -> int:
    """max{ k <= i : k in A_i }  (0 if none).  This single construction proves
    overspill, internal induction and internal completeness."""
    for k in range(i, -1, -1):
        if membership(k, i):
            return k
    return 0


def saturation_witness(conditions: Sequence[Callable[[int, int], bool]],
                       i: int, search: int = 200) -> Tuple[int, int]:
    """Diagonal for countable saturation: at coordinate i satisfy as many of the
    first conditions as that coordinate allows.  Returns (depth, witness)."""
    best_depth, best_x = -1, 0
    for n in range(min(i, len(conditions) - 1), -1, -1):
        for x in range(search):
            if all(conditions[k](x, i) for k in range(n + 1)):
                return n, x
        if best_depth < 0:
            best_depth, best_x = n, 0
    return max(best_depth, 0), best_x

def is_prime(n: int) -> bool:
    if n < 2:
        return False
    if n % 2 == 0:
        return n == 2
    d = 3
    while d * d <= n:
        if n % d == 0:
            return False
        d += 2
    return True


_PRIME_CACHE: List[int] = [2]


def nth_prime(k: int) -> int:
    """The k-th prime (0-indexed), with memoization."""
    n = _PRIME_CACHE[-1]
    while len(_PRIME_CACHE) <= k:
        n += 1
        if is_prime(n):
            _PRIME_CACHE.append(n)
    return _PRIME_CACHE[k]


def min_fac(n: int) -> int:
    if n < 2:
        return n
    d = 2
    while d * d <= n:
        if n % d == 0:
            return d
        d += 1
    return n

def composite_centre(i: int) -> int:
    """C = [i |-> i! + i//2], the middle of the composite run i!+2, ..., i!+i."""
    return math.factorial(i) + i // 2


def galaxy_window_is_prime_free(i: int, bandwidth: int) -> bool:
    """Is the whole window C(i) +- bandwidth composite?"""
    c = composite_centre(i)
    return all(not is_prime(c + delta) for delta in range(-bandwidth, bandwidth + 1))

def star_seq(a: Callable[[int], float], f: Seq) -> Callable[[int], float]:
    """The nonstandard extension of the real sequence a, evaluated at [f]."""
    return lambda i: a(f(i))


def standard_part_estimate(x: Callable[[int], float],
                           horizon: int = HORIZON) -> Tuple[float, float]:
    """Estimate the standard part of a hyperreal germ by the tail of its
    coordinates, together with the tail oscillation (0 means a genuine limit)."""
    tail = [x(i) for i in range(horizon // 2, horizon)]
    return sum(tail) / len(tail), max(tail) - min(tail)

       border:1px solid var(--line);font-size:.92rem;user-select:none}
  .tab.active{background:linear-gradient(180deg,#2b4a7a,#22355c);border-color:var(--accent)}
  .panel{background:var(--panel);border:1px solid var(--line);border-radius:14px;padding:18px;
         display:none}
  .panel.active{display:block}
  .row{display:flex;gap:18px;flex-wrap:wrap;align-items:flex-end;margin-bottom:12px}
  label{font-size:.82rem;color:var(--dim);display:block;margin-bottom:4px}
  select,input[type=range],input[type=number]{background:#0f142a;color:var(--ink);
       border:1px solid var(--line);border-radius:8px;padding:6px 8px;font-size:.9rem}
  input[type=range]{padding:0;width:220px}
  canvas{width:100%;background:#0b0f1e;border:1px solid var(--line);border-radius:10px}
  .verdict{margin-top:14px;padding:12px 14px;border-radius:10px;background:#101733;
           border-left:4px solid var(--accent);font-size:.95rem}
  .verdict b{color:var(--accent2)}
  .ok{color:var(--good);font-weight:600}
  .no{color:var(--bad);font-weight:600}
  .mono{font-family:ui-monospace,SFMono-Regular,Consolas,monospace;font-size:.86rem}
  .grid{display:grid;grid-template-columns:repeat(auto-fill,minmax(112px,1fr));gap:6px;margin-top:12px}
  .cell{padding:7px 4px;border-radius:8px;text-align:center;font-size:.78rem;
        border:1px solid var(--line);background:#0f142a}
  .cell.prime{background:#243d2a;border-color:#3f7a52;color:#a8f0c0}
  .cell.comp{background:#2a1d24;border-color:#6b3a46;color:#ffb3c0}
  .note{color:var(--dim);font-size:.85rem;margin-top:10px}
  table{width:100%;border-collapse:collapse;margin-top:10px;font-size:.88rem}
  th,td{border-bottom:1px solid var(--line);padding:6px 8px;text-align:left}
  th{color:var(--dim);font-weight:600}
</style>
</head>
<body>
<div class="wrap">
  <h1>The Ultrafilter Laboratory</h1>
  <p class="sub">A hypernatural is a sequence of ordinary naturals, two sequences naming the same
  number when they agree on a <i>large</i> set of coordinates. Every cofinite set is large, so a
  statement that holds from some coordinate onwards holds in the model. Explore what that means.</p>

  <div class="tabs">
    <div class="tab active" data-p="p1">1 · Germ comparator & galaxies</div>
    <div class="tab" data-p="p2">2 · Overspill: the diagonal witness</div>
    <div class="tab" data-p="p3">3 · Prime-free scales</div>
  </div>

  <!-- ---------------------------------------------------------------- -->
  <div class="panel active" id="p1">
    <div class="row">
      <div>
        <label>first germ  <span class="mono">[f]</span></label>
        <select id="f1"></select>
      </div>
      <div>
        <label>second germ  <span class="mono">[g]</span></label>
        <select id="g1"></select>
      </div>
      <div>
        <label>slope <span class="mono">r</span> (for staircase germs) : <span id="rval">1.30</span></label>
        <input type="range" id="rsl" min="0.2" max="3" step="0.01" value="1.3">
      </div>
      <div>
        <label>coordinates shown : <span id="nval">120</span></label>
        <input type="range" id="nsl" min="30" max="400" step="10" value="120">
      </div>
    </div>
    <canvas id="c1" width="1000" height="330"></canvas>
    <div class="verdict" id="v1"></div>
    <p class="note">The order is decided coordinatewise on a large set: if one sequence eventually
    stays below the other, it is smaller <i>as a hypernatural</i>, however wildly they behave at the
    start. Two germs share a <b>galaxy</b> when their difference stays bounded by an ordinary
    number; otherwise one is <b>far above</b> the other, and they measure different scales of
    infinity.</p>
  </div>

  <!-- ---------------------------------------------------------------- -->
  <div class="panel" id="p2">
    <div class="row">
      <div>
        <label>internal set  <span class="mono">Aₐ</span></label>
        <select id="setsel">
          <option value="mult">multiples of k</option>
          <option value="sq">perfect squares</option>
          <option value="prime">primes</option>
          <option value="half">numbers ≥ i/2</option>
        </select>
      </div>
      <div>
        <label>k : <span id="kval">3</span></label>
        <input type="range" id="ksl" min="2" max="12" step="1" value="3">
      </div>
      <div>
        <label>level to beat : <span id="lval">25</span></label>
        <input type="range" id="lsl" min="1" max="120" step="1" value="25">
      </div>
    </div>
    <canvas id="c2" width="1000" height="330"></canvas>
    <div class="verdict" id="v2"></div>
    <p class="note">Overspill: an internal set containing every ordinary natural must contain an
    infinite one. The witness is the <b>diagonal</b> <span class="mono">f(i) = max{k ≤ i : k ∈ Aₐ}</span> —
    each coordinate does only a finite search, but the bound grows with the coordinate, so the germ
    outruns every standard level. The same construction proves internal induction, the existence of
    internal maxima, and countable saturation.</p>
  </div>

  <!-- ---------------------------------------------------------------- -->
  <div class="panel" id="p3">
    <div class="row">
      <div>
        <label>coordinate i : <span id="ival">12</span></label>
        <input type="range" id="isl" min="4" max="24" step="1" value="12">
      </div>
      <div>
        <label>standard bandwidth m : <span id="mval">4</span></label>
        <input type="range" id="msl" min="1" max="10" step="1" value="4">
      </div>
    </div>
    <div class="verdict" id="v3"></div>
    <div class="grid" id="grid3"></div>
    <table id="t3">
      <tr><th>quantity</th><th>value</th></tr>
    </table>
    <p class="note">Since <span class="mono">j</span> divides <span class="mono">i! + j</span> for
    <span class="mono">2 ≤ j ≤ i</span>, the block
    <span class="mono">i!+2, …, i!+i</span> is a run of composites whose length grows without
    bound. Put a germ in the middle of that run,
    <span class="mono">C = [ i! + ⌊i/2⌋ ]</span>: for every ordinary bandwidth
    <span class="mono">m</span>, the whole window <span class="mono">C ± m</span> is composite
    from coordinate <span class="mono">2m+8</span> on. So no prime lies within a standard distance of
    <span class="mono">C</span>: an entire scale of the number system is prime-free.</p>
  </div>
</div>

<script>
/* ------------------------------------------------------------------ */
/* germ library                                                        */
const GERMS = [
  {id:'omega',   name:'ω = [i]',                 f:(i,r)=>i},
  {id:'shift',   name:'ω + 12',                  f:(i,r)=>i+12},
  {id:'double',  name:'2ω = [2i]',               f:(i,r)=>2*i},
  {id:'half',    name:'ω/2 = [⌊i/2⌋]',           f:(i,r)=>Math.floor(i/2)},
  {id:'stair',   name:'staircase [⌊i·r⌋]',       f:(i,r)=>Math.floor(i*r)},
  {id:'square',  name:'ω² = [i²]',               f:(i,r)=>i*i},
  {id:'wobble',  name:'wobbler [i + 8·(-1)^i]',  f:(i,r)=>Math.max(0,i+8*(i%2?-1:1))},
  {id:'const',   name:'standard 30',             f:(i,r)=>30},
];

function fillSelect(sel, initial){
  GERMS.forEach(g=>{const o=document.createElement('option');o.value=g.id;o.textContent=g.name;sel.appendChild(o);});
  sel.value=initial;
}
const f1=document.getElementById('f1'), g1=document.getElementById('g1');
fillSelect(f1,'omega'); fillSelect(g1,'stair');

function germ(id){ return GERMS.find(g=>g.id===id).f; }

/* threshold at which a predicate stops failing, within the horizon */
function threshold(pred, N){
  let last=-1;
  for(let i=0;i<=N;i++) if(!pred(i)) last=i;
  return last>=N ? null : last+1;
}

/* ------------------------------------------------------------------ */
/* tabs                                                                */
document.querySelectorAll('.tab').forEach(t=>{
  t.onclick=()=>{
    document.querySelectorAll('.tab').forEach(x=>x.classList.remove('active'));
    document.querySelectorAll('.panel').forEach(x=>x.classList.remove('active'));
    t.classList.add('active');
    document.getElementById(t.dataset.p).classList.add('active');
  };
});

/* ------------------------------------------------------------------ */
/* panel 1                                                             */
const c1=document.getElementById('c1'), x1=c1.getContext('2d');

function drawSeries(ctx,W,H,series,N,title){
  ctx.clearRect(0,0,W,H);
  let hi=1;
  series.forEach(s=>{for(let i=0;i<N;i++) hi=Math.max(hi,s.v[i]);});
  const padL=54,padB=30,padT=22,padR=14;
  const sx=i=>padL+(i/(N-1))*(W-padL-padR);
  const sy=y=>H-padB-(y/hi)*(H-padB-padT);
  ctx.strokeStyle='#2a3352'; ctx.lineWidth=1;
  ctx.beginPath(); ctx.moveTo(padL,padT); ctx.lineTo(padL,H-padB); ctx.lineTo(W-padR,H-padB); ctx.stroke();
  ctx.fillStyle='#96a0c2'; ctx.font='12px ui-monospace,monospace';
  ctx.fillText('0',padL-14,H-padB+4);
  ctx.fillText(String(Math.round(hi)),8,padT+10);
  ctx.fillText('coordinate i',W/2-40,H-8);
  ctx.fillText(title,padL+6,14);
  series.forEach(s=>{
    ctx.strokeStyle=s.c; ctx.lineWidth=2; ctx.beginPath();
    for(let i=0;i<N;i++){ const X=sx(i),Y=sy(s.v[i]); i?ctx.lineTo(X,Y):ctx.moveTo(X,Y); }
    ctx.stroke();
    ctx.fillStyle=s.c; ctx.fillText(s.n, W-padR-160, padT+14+s.k*16);
  });
}

function update1(){
  const r=parseFloat(document.getElementById('rsl').value);
  const N=parseInt(document.getElementById('nsl').value);
  document.getElementById('rval').textContent=r.toFixed(2);
  document.getElementById('nval').textContent=N;
  const F=germ(f1.value), G=germ(g1.value);
  const vf=[],vg=[];
  for(let i=0;i<N;i++){vf.push(F(i,r));vg.push(G(i,r));}
  drawSeries(x1,c1.width,c1.height,
    [{v:vf,c:'#7cc7ff',n:'[f]',k:0},{v:vg,c:'#ffcf6b',n:'[g]',k:1}],N,
    'representing sequences');

  const HOR=Math.max(N,600);
  const lt=threshold(i=>F(i,r)<G(i,r),HOR);
  const gt=threshold(i=>G(i,r)<F(i,r),HOR);
  const eq=threshold(i=>F(i,r)===G(i,r),HOR);
  let order;
  if(lt!==null) order=`<span class="ok">[f] < [g]</span>, certified from coordinate <b>${lt}</b>`;
  else if(gt!==null) order=`<span class="ok">[g] < [f]</span>, certified from coordinate <b>${gt}</b>`;
  else if(eq!==null) order=`<span class="ok">[f] = [g]</span>, certified from coordinate <b>${eq}</b>`;
  else order=`the two sequences keep crossing inside the horizon — the ultrafilter still decides the order, but no cofinite certificate is visible here`;

  // galaxy test: is the drift eventually bounded by an ordinary number?
  const drift=i=>Math.abs(F(i,r)-G(i,r));
  const maxOn=(a,b)=>{let m=0;for(let i=a;i<=b;i++)m=Math.max(m,drift(i));return m;};
  const dMid=maxOn(Math.floor(HOR/4),Math.floor(HOR/2));
  const dTail=maxOn(Math.floor(HOR/2),HOR);
  const bounded = dTail<=dMid;                 // no growth on the tail
  const far = !bounded && (lt!==null || gt!==null);

  const gal = bounded
    ? `<span class="ok">same galaxy</span>: the drift never exceeds the ordinary number <b>${dTail}</b>, however far you go`
    : `<span class="no">different galaxies</span>: the drift keeps growing (<b>${dMid}</b> by coordinate ${Math.floor(HOR/2)}, <b>${dTail}</b> by ${HOR}) and outgrows every ordinary bound`;
  const farTxt = far
    ? ' — one is <b>far above</b> the other, so they measure different scales of infinity'
    : '';

  const unlF=[...Array(10).keys()].every(n=>threshold(i=>F(i,r)>n,HOR)!==null);
  const unlG=[...Array(10).keys()].every(n=>threshold(i=>G(i,r)>n,HOR)!==null);

  document.getElementById('v1').innerHTML =
    `<div>Order: ${order}</div>
     <div style="margin-top:6px">Scale: ${gal}${farTxt}</div>
     <div style="margin-top:6px">Unlimited (bigger than every ordinary number)?
       [f]: ${unlF?'<span class="ok">yes</span>':'<span class="no">no</span>'}   
       [g]: ${unlG?'<span class="ok">yes</span>':'<span class="no">no</span>'}</div>`;
}
['f1','g1','rsl','nsl'].forEach(id=>document.getElementById(id).addEventListener('input',update1));

/* ------------------------------------------------------------------ */
/* panel 2                                                             */
const c2=document.getElementById('c2'), x2=c2.getContext('2d');
function isPrime(n){ if(n<2)return false; if(n%2===0)return n===2;
  for(let d=3;d*d<=n;d+=2) if(n%d===0) return false; return true; }

function member(kind,k,x,i){
  if(kind==='mult') return x%k===0;
  if(kind==='sq')   return Number.isInteger(Math.sqrt(x));
  if(kind==='prime')return isPrime(x);
  return x>=i/2;
}
function update2(){
  const kind=document.getElementById('setsel').value;
  const k=parseInt(document.getElementById('ksl').value);
  const L=parseInt(document.getElementById('lsl').value);
  document.getElementById('kval').textContent=k;
  document.getElementById('lval').textContent=L;
  const N=220, v=[];
  for(let i=0;i<N;i++){
    let best=0;
    for(let x=i;x>=0;x--){ if(member(kind,k,x,i)){best=x;break;} }
    v.push(best);
  }
  drawSeries(x2,c2.width,c2.height,
    [{v:v,c:'#6ee7a8',n:'diagonal witness',k:0},
     {v:Array.from({length:N},()=>L),c:'#ff8b8b',n:'standard level',k:1}],N,
    'f(i) = max{ k ≤ i : k ∈ A_i }');
  const thr=threshold(i=>{
    let best=0; for(let x=i;x>=0;x--){ if(member(kind,k,x,i)){best=x;break;} } return best>L;
  },N-1);
  document.getElementById('v2').innerHTML = thr!==null
    ? `The witness passes the level <b>${L}</b> from coordinate <b>${thr}</b> and never returns below it:
       a cofinite set of coordinates, hence a large one. Raise the level as high as you like — the
       witness always eventually beats it, so <span class="ok">the diagonal germ is an infinite element
       of the internal set</span>. That is overspill.`
    : `<span class="no">No certificate inside this horizon.</span> Either the set is too sparse near the
       diagonal, or the level is too high for the coordinates shown — push the horizon up in your head:
       the theorem still applies whenever the set contains every ordinary natural.`;
}
['setsel','ksl','lsl'].forEach(id=>document.getElementById(id).addEventListener('input',update2));

/* ------------------------------------------------------------------ */
/* panel 3                                                             */
function factorialBig(n){ let r=1n; for(let j=2n;j<=BigInt(n);j++) r*=j; return r; }
function smallestFactor(n){           // n is a BigInt
  if(n%2n===0n) return 2n;
  for(let d=3n; d*d<=n && d<200000n; d+=2n) if(n%d===0n) return d;
  return null;                        // no small factor found
}
function update3(){
  const i=parseInt(document.getElementById('isl').value);
  const m=parseInt(document.getElementById('msl').value);
  document.getElementById('ival').textContent=i;
  document.getElementById('mval').textContent=m;
  const fact=factorialBig(i);
  const C=fact+BigInt(Math.floor(i/2));
  const grid=document.getElementById('grid3'); grid.innerHTML='';
  let allComposite=true;
  for(let d=-m; d<=m; d++){
    const n=C+BigInt(d);
    const sf=smallestFactor(n);
    const cell=document.createElement('div');
    cell.className='cell '+(sf?'comp':'prime');
    cell.innerHTML=`C${d===0?'':(d>0?'+'+d:d)}<br><span class="mono">${sf?('÷'+sf):'prime?'}</span>`;
    grid.appendChild(cell);
    if(!sf) allComposite=false;
  }
  const t=document.getElementById('t3');
  t.innerHTML='<tr><th>quantity</th><th>value</th></tr>';
  const rows=[
    ['coordinate i', i],
    ['centre C(i) = i! + ⌊i/2⌋', C.toString().length>36 ? C.toString().slice(0,36)+'…' : C.toString()],
    ['digits of C(i)', C.toString().length],
    ['guaranteed composite run i!+2 … i!+i', (i-1)+' consecutive numbers'],
    ['window width 2m+1', 2*m+1],
    ['theory: run swallows the window once', 'i ≥ 2m+8 = '+(2*m+8)],
  ];
  rows.forEach(([a,b])=>{const tr=document.createElement('tr');
    tr.innerHTML=`<td>${a}</td><td class="mono">${b}</td>`;t.appendChild(tr);});
  document.getElementById('v3').innerHTML = allComposite
    ? `Every number within distance <b>${m}</b> of <span class="mono">C(${i})</span> is
       <span class="ok">composite</span> — each has a visible small factor.
       Since this persists for all larger coordinates, <b>no prime is within a standard distance of
       C</b>: the entire galaxy of C is prime-free.`
    : `<span class="no">At this coordinate the window is not yet fully inside the composite run</span>
       (need i ≥ 2m+8 = ${2*m+8}). Increase i and watch the run swallow the window for good.`;
}
['isl','msl'].forEach(id=>document.getElementById(id).addEventListener('input',update3));

update1(); update2(); update3();
</script>
</body>
</html>
"
    },
    {
      "title": "Robinson's Telescope: Limits, Divergence and Compactness as Evaluations at Infinite Indices",
      "description": "An interactive rendering of Robinson's criterion, which replaces the epsilon-N definition of a limit by a single evaluation: a real sequence converges to L exactly when its extension has standard part L at every infinite index. The reader picks a sequence -- convergent, alternating, damped alternating, sin(n), a slow divergence, or an equidistributed fractional part -- and an infinite index from omega, [2i], [2i+1], [i^2] and a golden-ratio staircase, and sees the extension plotted with its rounded value, alongside a table of the rounded values at all five indices. Agreement across indices certifies convergence; disagreement between two indices is a complete certificate of divergence; and a bounded sequence always yields a finite value that can be rounded to a real number, which is exactly the nonstandard proof of the Bolzano-Weierstrass theorem.",
      "html": "<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
<meta charset="utf-8">
<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
<title>Robinson's Telescope: limits as evaluations at infinite indices</title>
<style>
  :root{--bg:#0d1020;--panel:#161c2f;--ink:#e9edf9;--dim:#939dbe;--accent:#8fd0ff;
        --accent2:#ffd479;--good:#6fe6a6;--bad:#ff9090;--line:#28304d}
  *{box-sizing:border-box}
  body{margin:0;background:var(--bg);color:var(--ink);line-height:1.55;
       font-family:"Segoe UI",Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif}
  .wrap{max-width:1020px;margin:0 auto;padding:22px}
  h1{font-size:1.5rem;margin:0 0 4px}
  p.sub{color:var(--dim);margin:0 0 16px}
  .panel{background:var(--panel);border:1px solid var(--line);border-radius:14px;padding:18px}
  .row{display:flex;gap:20px;flex-wrap:wrap;align-items:flex-end;margin-bottom:14px}
  label{display:block;font-size:.82rem;color:var(--dim);margin-bottom:4px}
  select,input[type=range]{background:#0b0f22;color:var(--ink);border:1px solid var(--line);
        border-radius:8px;padding:6px 8px;font-size:.9rem}
  input[type=range]{padding:0;width:230px}
  canvas{width:100%;background:#080c1a;border:1px solid var(--line);border-radius:10px}
  table{width:100%;border-collapse:collapse;margin-top:14px;font-size:.9rem}
  th,td{border-bottom:1px solid var(--line);padding:7px 9px;text-align:left}
  th{color:var(--dim)}
  .mono{font-family:ui-monospace,Consolas,monospace}
  .verdict{margin-top:14px;padding:12px 14px;border-radius:10px;background:#101a33;
           border-left:4px solid var(--accent)}
  .ok{color:var(--good);font-weight:600}.no{color:var(--bad);font-weight:600}
  .note{color:var(--dim);font-size:.86rem;margin-top:12px}
</style>
</head>
<body>
<div class="wrap">
  <h1>Robinson's Telescope</h1>
  <p class="sub">A real sequence extends to infinite indices: at the hypernatural
  <span class="mono">H = [f]</span> its value is the germ <span class="mono">[ i ↦ a<sub>f(i)</sub> ]</span>.
  A sequence converges to <span class="mono">L</span> exactly when this value is infinitely close to
  <span class="mono">L</span> at <em>every</em> infinite index — so limits become evaluations, and
  divergence becomes a disagreement between two infinite indices.</p>

  <div class="panel">
    <div class="row">
      <div>
        <label>sequence <span class="mono">a<sub>n</sub></span></label>
        <select id="seq">
          <option value="conv">1 + 1/(n+1)  (converges)</option>
          <option value="alt">(-1)^n  (diverges, bounded)</option>
          <option value="damped">(-1)^n / (n+1)  (converges to 0)</option>
          <option value="sin">sin(n)  (bounded, no limit)</option>
          <option value="log">log(n+2)/ (n+2)^0.3  (diverges to +∞)</option>
          <option value="frac">frac(n·√2) - 1/2  (equidistributed)</option>
        </select>
      </div>
      <div>
        <label>infinite index <span class="mono">H</span></label>
        <select id="idx">
          <option value="id">ω = [i]</option>
          <option value="even">[2i]</option>
          <option value="odd">[2i+1]</option>
          <option value="sq">[i²]</option>
          <option value="stair">[⌊i·φ⌋]</option>
        </select>
      </div>
      <div>
        <label>coordinates shown : <span id="nval">300</span></label>
        <input type="range" id="nsl" min="60" max="1200" step="20" value="300">
      </div>
    </div>

    <canvas id="cv" width="1000" height="320"></canvas>
    <div class="verdict" id="verdict"></div>

    <table id="tbl"></table>

    <p class="note">The table evaluates the sequence at several infinite indices at once. If all of
    them round to the same real number, that number is the limit — a single universally quantified
    statement replaces the whole ε–N dance. If two indices round differently, the sequence has no
    limit, and you have <em>witnessed</em> the divergence rather than inferred it. If a bounded sequence
    is evaluated at an infinite index the result is always a finite quantity, so it can be rounded to a
    real number, and that real number is automatically a cluster point: this is the Bolzano–Weierstrass
    theorem, reduced to rounding.</p>
  </div>
</div>

<script>
const SEQ = {
  conv:  n => 1 + 1/(n+1),
  alt:   n => Math.pow(-1,n),
  damped:n => Math.pow(-1,n)/(n+1),
  sin:   n => Math.sin(n),
  log:   n => Math.log(n+2)/Math.pow(n+2,0.3),
  frac:  n => { const x=n*Math.SQRT2; return (x-Math.floor(x))-0.5; }
};

Imagine a number $\omega$ that is bigger than $1$, bigger than $10^{100}$, bigger than every
number you could ever write down — and yet is a perfectly ordinary integer: it has a successor,
a parity, a prime factorization, a remainder modulo $7$. This page builds such a number system
from scratch, shows you which theorems of ordinary arithmetic survive inside it, and lets you
poke at the machinery yourself.

By the end you will have seen, and been able to verify interactively:

- a construction of infinite integers out of nothing but sequences of ordinary ones;
- a **transfer principle** proving that no first-order statement can distinguish the new number
  system from the old one;
- the sharp dividing line between the **internal** sets, for which classical theorems survive,
  and the **external** ones, for which they fail spectacularly;
- that the new system has exactly as many elements as there are real numbers, and is stratified
  into a *dense* order of scales of infinity called **galaxies**;
- that primes are unbounded in the model but **absent from entire scales**;
- and, coming back home, that limits and compactness in ordinary analysis become simple algebra
  at infinite indices.

---

## 1. Building an infinite integer

The recipe has one ingredient: a notion of *largeness* for sets of coordinates.

> A family $\mathcal{U}$ of subsets of $\mathbb{N}$ is a **nonprincipal ultrafilter** if:
> $\mathbb{N}$ is large; the intersection of two large sets is large; of any set and its
> complement exactly one is large; and no finite set is large (hence every cofinite set is large).

Now define a **hypernatural** to be a sequence $f:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}$, where two sequences
$f$ and $g$ name the same number when $\{i : f(i)=g(i)\}$ is large. Write $[f]$ for the number
named by $f$. Addition, multiplication and order are coordinatewise:
$$[f] < [g] \iff \{i : f(i) < g(i)\}\ \text{is large}.$$

Two inhabitants matter immediately. Each ordinary number $n$ appears as the constant sequence
$n^\ast$. And the identity sequence gives
$$\omega = [\,i \mapsto i\,],$$
which beats every $n^\ast$, because $\{i : i > n\}$ is cofinite and therefore large. That is our
infinite integer.

<details>
<summary><b>Why does an ultrafilter exist, and why can't I see one?</b></summary>

Start with the family of cofinite sets — it satisfies everything except the "exactly one of
$S$, $S^c$" rule. [Zorn's lemma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zorn%27s_lemma) extends it to a
maximal filter, and maximality is exactly the missing rule. The catch: the extension involves
infinitely many arbitrary choices, and it is a theorem that no nonprincipal ultrafilter on
$\mathbb{N}$ can be defined explicitly. Fortunately, none of the constructions on this page ever
need to *know* the ultrafilter: every one of them produces a statement that holds for **all
sufficiently large coordinates**, and cofinite sets are large in every choice of $\mathcal{U}$.
That is the trick which makes the interactive panels below honest rather than hand-waving.
</details>

---

## 3. Nothing you can say detects the difference

> **Transfer Principle.** A first-order sentence — one built from $0$, $+$, $\times$, $<$ and
> quantifiers *over numbers* — holds in the new number system if and only if it holds in the old
> one.

So the hypernaturals satisfy commutativity, discreteness of the order, existence of Euclidean
division, "every number $>1$ has a prime divisor", "there are infinitely many primes"… every
theorem of ordinary first-order arithmetic, verbatim.

<details>
<summary><b>Proof sketch (induction on formulas)</b></summary>

One proves the stronger statement that for any formula $\varphi(x_1,\dots,x_k)$,
$$\varphi([f_1],\dots,[f_k])\ \text{holds}\quad\iff\quad \{i : \varphi(f_1(i),\dots,f_k(i))\ \text{holds}\}\ \text{is large}.$$
Atomic formulas hold by definition of the lifted relations. Conjunction uses closure of largeness
under intersection. **Negation is the crucial step** and uses the rule that exactly one of $S$,
$S^c$ is large: "not almost-everywhere true" becomes "almost-everywhere false", which is why we
need an *ultra*filter and not merely a filter. The existential step assembles a witness sequence
out of coordinatewise witnesses (this is where the axiom of choice enters). A sentence has no free
variables, so the right-hand side is a constant condition, and the theorem drops out.
</details>

If everything transfers, where does the strangeness hide? In the **sets**.

---

## 4. Internal versus external: the real dividing line

A subset of the model is **internal** when it, too, is a sequence: given ordinary sets
$A_0, A_1, A_2, \dots \subseteq \mathbb{N}$, the internal set they define contains exactly those
$[f]$ with $\{i : f(i) \in A_i\}$ large. Everything else is **external**.

The single most important construction in the subject is the *diagonal witness*, which you already
met in panel 2 of the laboratory:
$$ f(i) \;=\; \max\{\,k \le i \;:\; k \in A_i\,\}. $$
Each coordinate performs a finite search, but the search window grows, so the resulting germ
outruns every ordinary number.

{{algorithm:0}}

That one algorithm proves four theorems:

> **Overspill.** An internal set containing every ordinary number contains an infinite one.
>
> **Underspill.** An internal set containing every infinite number contains an ordinary one.
>
> **Internal induction.** An internal set containing $0$ and closed under successor is everything.
>
> **Internal completeness.** A nonempty internal set bounded above has a greatest element (replace
> the window $k\le i$ by $k \le b(i)$, the bound).

And it has an immediate, startling corollary: **no internal set consists exactly of the ordinary
numbers**. From inside the model, the boundary between finite and infinite is invisible.

<details>
<summary><b>Overspill in three lines</b></summary>

Suppose the internal set contains every $n^\ast$; then for each $n$, $n \in A_i$ for almost all $i$.
For any $n$, on the (large) intersection of $\{i : n+1 \in A_i\}$ with the cofinite set
$\{i : i \ge n+1\}$ we get $f(i) \ge n+1$. Hence $[f]$ beats every ordinary number. And on the
large set where $1 \in A_i$ and $i \ge 1$ we get $f(i) \in A_i$, so $[f]$ is in the set. $\blacksquare$
</details>

Now the punchline of the whole subject: run the classical set-theoretic principles of $\mathbb{N}$
through the internal/external filter and watch them separate cleanly.

{{demo:1}}

| principle | internal version | external version |
|---|---|---|
| least number principle | **holds** — take $\min A_i$ coordinatewise | **fails**: if $H$ is infinite so is $H-1$, so the infinite numbers have no least element |
| induction | **holds** — via the diagonal witness | **fails**: "is standard" contains $0$, is closed under successor, and misses $\omega$ |
| bounded sets have suprema | **holds**, and the supremum is attained | **fails**: the ordinary numbers are bounded by $\omega$ but have *no* least upper bound |
